author: Peter Wildeford
text: Multi-agent AI safety is going to be hella weird and hard [quoting Moritz Weckbecker: 'We found a new way to misalign an entire AI agent network by compromising just one agent. Subliminal messaging with no malicious content in any message so current defenses can't detect it. We call it: Thought Virus.']
suggestedEngagement: The 'no malicious content detectable' property is what makes Thought Virus architecturally significant — it breaks the assumption that content-level filtering at the perimeter is sufficient. In a mesh of agents, infection through legitimate-looking reasoning chains is a fundamentally different threat model than prompt injection. Are there known mitigations that operate at the agent-communication layer rather than the content layer?

The blast-radius implication is the hardest part: if one compromised agent can silently propagate misalignment to its peers, the whole 'blast radius = single agent' assumption that most enterprise governance frameworks rely on collapses. What isolation primitive do you think actually contains this — message attestation, capability-scoped subagents, or something else?

Ask if he sees parallels to the Byzantine fault tolerance literature — that field has well-studied proofs about what fraction of compromised nodes can poison a consensus system. Multi-agent safety might need similar formal guarantees before enterprise deployment is safe at scale.

author: Ashpreet Bedi
text: Systems Engineering: Building Agentic Software That Works — argues that building agentic software is systems engineering across five layers: (1) Agent Engineering — model, system instructions, tool configs, handoffs, context management; (2) Data Engineering — schemas, structured querying, storage pipelines; (3) Security Engineering — auth, RBAC, governance, data isolation, audit trails, JWT-backed tool permissions; (4) Interface Engineering — REST API, Slack, MCP surfaces with consistent auth; (5) Infrastructure Engineering — containers, cloud, horizontal scaling. Systems engineering is the discipline of making these parts work together.
suggestedEngagement: The five-layer framing is clean and maps well to how enterprise deployments actually fail — but in practice, layers 3 (security) and 4 (interface) tend to get bolted on after the fact rather than designed in from the start. Is there a specific sequencing you'd recommend for teams building greenfield vs. retrofitting security and interface controls onto existing agent logic?

The JWT-backed permissions for tools is the right instinct — capability-level authorization rather than just agent-level auth. The gap most teams hit is governance: who owns the tool permission manifest and how does it get reviewed when the tool surface evolves? Have you seen a clean pattern for that in Agno deployments?

The MCP surface in Interface Engineering is the most interesting inclusion — it signals that agents themselves are now first-class API consumers. That changes the auth model significantly (agents can't do OAuth interactively). Are you seeing teams build service-account patterns for agent-to-MCP auth, or is there a better primitive emerging?
